parts.text:
33 Which two units are used to define the coulomb?
A
ampere and second
B
ampere and volt
C
volt and ohm
D
volt and second

hints: Notice the coulomb $\text{C}$ is the unit of electric charge $Q$, while the ampere $\text{A}$ is the SI base unit of electric current $I$.
Recall the link between current, charge and time: $I = Q/t$, where time $t$ is measured in seconds.
Rearrange to $Q = It$ and check which two units multiply together to make one coulomb.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the coulomb is the unit of charge $Q$, so find the defining equation for charge.
State the governing physics: electric current is rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$.
Insert units with unit check: $[Q] = [I] \times [t] = \text{A} \times \text{s}$, so $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$.
Therefore the coulomb is defined using the ampere and the second. This is option A.

A.explanation: Charge is current multiplied by time, so $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A} \times 1 \text{ s}$.

B.explanation: Volt is the unit of potential difference, and ampere times volt gives power in watt, not charge.

C.explanation: Volt divided by ohm gives current in ampere by $I = V/R$, so this pair does not combine to give coulomb.

D.explanation: Volt times second gives weber for magnetic flux, not coulomb for electric charge.
